SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.
  • The agency noted Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022.
  • Federal prosecutors in Latest York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.

The agency noted Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022. A federal court granted a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze and expedited discovery to halt what the SEC called an ongoing scheme.

Federal prosecutors in Latest York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases. The SEC and CFTC suits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, and the CFTC stated the court has appointed Kevin B. Duff as temporary receiver to take control of the companies and the individual defendants’ assets.

In a recent development, according to the SEC’s complaint, Williams and Johnson sold limited partnership interests in private funds through a network of promoters, including to Williams’s former investment advisory clients. They promised a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm that supposedly returned at least 6% every month by trading foreign exchange.

It has been revealed that investor money, the pitch went, would first be converted into a crypto asset and then used for that arbitrage. The complaint does not name bitcoin as the asset. It notes about $109 million of the roughly $210 million raised from July 2022 to September 2025 was sent to the fund’s Coinbase account and converted.

Of that, more than $56 million went to personal crypto accounts held by Williams, Johnson and a relief defendant, according to the complaint. About $40 million ended up on three platforms where some of it was used to trade other crypto assets, but little to no money was used to trade FX. After October 2025, the scheme raised about $350 million, and none of it was sent to Coinbase.

Industry observers note that the SEC noted the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi payments to earlier investors and moved more than $220 million to themselves. The money paid for exotic cars, expensive homes, private air travel and other businesses they owned, and helped feed Johnson’s gambling. Promoters took more than $50 million.

Industry observers note that anderson is accused of producing fake financial reports, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report from a supposedly independent firm. The SEC mentioned the documents falsely claimed the returns had been verified against bank and brokerage records. It said Anderson did no audit work, was not independent and had a financial stake in the scheme.

Prosecutors in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The FBI arrested Williams in Kokomo, Indiana, and Johnson in Gilbert, Arizona, on Wednesday. Prosecutors put the total raised at more than $600 million.

It has been revealed that “As alleged, Phillip Patrick Williams and Devin Allen Johnson promised to use investor funds for profitable foreign exchange currency trading,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Williams and Johnson instead stole hundreds of millions of dollars from their investors for personal expenses and to pay off earlier investors in a Ponzi-like fashion.”.

The CFTC put the Ponzi at more than $550 million from at least 2,100 participants and said defendants kept soliciting money through at least October 2026. Its complaint seeks restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties, trading bans and a permanent injunction. The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties.

According to recent reports, the case follows other recent enforcement actions tied to crypto-branded fraud. The SEC charged two companies in a $130 million crypto trading scheme last month, and Upcoming York sought a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of the NovaTech Ponzi scheme. In August, the CFTC charged Goliath Ventures with a $400 million bitcoin fraud.

Anne McKinley, acting associate director of the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office, remarked the promise of “a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money.”.

Finishing Touch is an underrated brand. I previously included the brand’s electric shaver with a built-in LED ring light to illuminate hairs I wouldn't usually see in my bathroom. This device works great if you have sensitive skin that's easily irritated. It's gentle enough to use daily, and I love keeping mine on hand at the office to check my face before walking into a meeting.

The only caveat is Flawless is a razor, so it cuts hair at the top layer of skin, meaning hair will grow back relatively fast. So, as long as you don't mind regular trims, this is an epic choice.

After two years of on-and-off testing, Flamingo still makes my favorite razor. Its sharp blades that don’t tug or pull at my sensitive skin elevate Flamingo to the top of my shower routine.

In a recent development, the brand suggests replacing the blades every four to six weeks, but each blade lasts me closer to eight weeks, meaning a regular four-pack of blades lasts me approximately 32 weeks (eight months) before becoming dull. Plus, this razor set is comfy to use while shaving down to my ankles. It curves along my kneecaps and pits with ease, and it hasn’t caused any nicks or ingrown hairs along my bikini line.

I’ll continue using Flamingo, and at just $16, you can also enjoy smooth skin which includes the razor, four blades, and a holder that fits neatly in cramped spaces like my Fresh York City shower.

While I don't mind using a traditional manual razor or dermaplaning, it's worth spending a little extra on this electric device, claims Wohlner. This Philips electric razor has a large head and self-sharpening blade to rapidly remove facial hair. Wohlner's been using this facial hair removal tool for hairs and considers it the most effective method for eliminating stubborn upper lip and chin hairs. "While it's too big to remove hair on my brows, it's awesome for those larger areas of the face when you're short on time and want to look smooth and stubble-free," she says.

Industry observers note that many other tools can irritate, especially around the upper lip area, which occasionally turns into bumps. This shaver has a hypoallergenic stainless steel head that doesn’t irritate sensitive skin, quickly removing unwanted hair in a single pass without causing pain or discomfort. This device keeps Wohlner's face smooth, and it always glides over the skin effortlessly without leaving it red and raw. It even comes with a built-in mirror in the cap to touch-up on the go.

Pro tip: The large shaver head does tend to get clogged after a few uses, which can be prevented if you wipe it down with alcohol after every use. Taking care of your device will ensure you get the closest shave and that it lasts for years.

The idea of gliding a sharp razor across my face was initially intimidating, but I haven't scratched myself since using the Dermaflash. Unlike cheaper options with dull blades, the Dermaflash provides the most professional-grade shave I've ever experienced while testing dozens of dermaplaning tools. The sharp blade features proprietary Microfine Edges, which are tiny corrugations that get super close to my face without any discomfort.

Most dermaplaning tools only have simple blades, but Dermaflash features a gentle pulsing technology that further removes peach fuzz and dead skin cells instantly and safely, making it handy for beginners and seasoned dermaplaning owners alike. My results rival pro treatments without the hassle of going to a spa and without the excessive upkeep cost. This tool easily glides across my face, which would normally be a challenge with cheaper, manual dermaplaning tools. Since using this device, I noticed my face cream sinks in quickly, and my foundation looks even more natural.

Sources indicate that I try to use this tool every two weeks to maintain my smooth results, but TBH, I use it monthly, which is better for my wallet. The brand advises swapping out the blade after every use for the smoothest results, so anything to stretch my beauty budget is always a win. FWIW: Even a monthly treatment prevents my makeup from pilling, so this tool will remain a consistent part of my routine.

Sugaring is epic because the paste only sticks to the hair, not the skin. It's far less painful than waxing and easier to apply.

In a recent development, I've previously only done professional sugaring, but the at-home process is the same. After heating the roller in the microwave, I apply the stick directly to the area I want sugared, lay down a strip, and pull it off in the opposite direction of the hair growth. The fabric strips are a little big to use on my face, especially on the chin or upper lip, but I can cut them in half, and they work perfectly.

Most sugaring wax is packaged in a tub that can tip over and cause a huge, sticky mess. Schick comes in a deodorant-like stick that easily rolls onto my skin. I like to warm the stick up in the microwave in 5-second increments until the paste has a honey-like consistency. I also need a light layer of sugaring wax to achieve the same results as other alternatives, meaning my roller can last for a few months.

It has been revealed that I initially missed a few hairs, so I had to follow up with a fresh swipe of sugaring paste. With some practice, my technique improved over time, and soon enough, it only took me a few minutes to wax the lower half of my face. At just $13 a wand, this at-home technique is much cheaper than going to a salon where I'd easily pay double the price, and for that alone, I'll continue using this kit.

It has been revealed that this hair removal cream isn't the Nair you grew up on. It's a prescription-strength cream specifically formulated to slow hair growth on the face. The key ingredients include eflornithine (6%), which blocks the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) that stimulates hair growth. Each batch is compounded together shortly before shipping, ensuring maximum potency.

Sources indicate that I've tried many hair removal creams, which sometimes cause redness and irritation, so I was worried Musely would be a problem. Musely provides instant hair-free results, and I noticed my regrowth is slower and my skin remains smoother with regular use, compared to other creams I’ve tried. It has a light tingling sensation, letting me know the cream is working. Unlike cheaper drugstore alternatives, Musely hasn't irritated my skin. It also doesn't have a super aggressive chemical smell like other alternatives I tested, and that alone is a win in my book.

The major downside of hair removal creams, including Musely, is that I have to adjust when I use my tretinoin prescription around hair removal days. After Musely hair removal, I typically wait a few days before safely applying my tretinoin cream. Otherwise, I might experience redness, irritation, and over-exfoliate my skin. Musely is a worthwhile product, but I prefer dermaplaning or shaving because I value acne-free skin over a fast-acting, pain-free hair removal process.

Your hair color, skin color, and hair thickness helps determine your best facial hair removal method, states dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. Also be real about your pain tolerance and bandwidth because the best method for removing facial hair is the one you'll consistently use to maintain smooth results. Also, think about investing in an electric hair removal device to speed up your primping routine and, of course, stick to your budget. Our suggestions start at just $10.

They are epic when you have dark hair and a fair to medium complexion; particularly those with thick, coarse and unruly dark chin, upper lip, and sideburn hair. But if you're a four or deeper on the Fitzpatrick Scale like me, you should skip using at-home laser hair removal devices. "You want to receive the right treatment that does not harm your skin," dermatologist Jeanine Downie, MD, previously told WH.

Recent findings suggest that they work by slowing hair growth and reducing strand thickness by using highly concentrated light to penetrate hair follicles and inhibit future hair growth. While laser hair removal isn't exactly permanent, it can effectively slow hair growth. This is my go-to hair removal method because of the low upkeep. I can easily go 4-6 weeks between my sessions, but TBH, I'll stretch it to every 8 weeks. This method helps promote cell turnover and collagen production plus minimizes dark spots and uneven skin texture, dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD, told WH. "When your skin is hairless and buildup-free, it looks super toned and bright," Dr. Shirazi remarked.

Recent findings suggest that since dermaplaning cuts the hairs at the top layer of skin, they'll grow back quicker than laser hair removal or waxing, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. So be ready to use this technique 1-4 times monthly, depending on how fast your hair regrows.

These creams typically contain ingredients like eflornithine, calcium hydroxide, calcium thioglycolate, sodium hydroxide, and sodium thioglycolate to dissolve keratin bond structures of strands, making them pain-free alternatives to tweezing, waxing, and sugaring. Let the cream sit for a few minutes, then wipe it away to reveal smoother skin. Recent findings suggest that these are best for removing hair from a small area of the face, like your eyebrows, chin, and upper lip. Recent findings suggest that ultimately, opt for the electric devices if you want a fast and powerful tool that lasts for years and don't mind the upfront cost. Choose a manual tool if you would rather save the cash for other beauty products, like an LED face mask or a red light therapy device for hair growth.

I also consulted dermatologists and associate commerce editor Lily Wohlner, about her no-fail recommendations to share the best facial hair removal methods for women worth using in 2025.

When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that though perhaps not well known outside France, Vincent Darré is one of Paris’s most familiar figures—always on the scene, day and night. The impish designer rarely just enters a room; he bounces in, impeccably dressed, with an infectious laugh and beautiful manners. At home in the worlds of fashion, society, art, and design, he is welcome at every table, always ready with a clever remark, a kind word, and no shortage of creative energy.

According to recent reports, from his early days in fashion, which included stints at Moschino and Ungaro and a close, yearslong collaboration with none other than Karl Lagerfeld, Darré has followed a singular path, turning his creative energies to furniture and interiors with the opening of his own studio, Maison Darré, in 2008. A pair of recently completed Paris hotels—L’Aventure, at the foot of the Arc de Triomphe, and Hôtel Le Magnifique, in the heart of Montparnasse—are propelling him onto the design scene in a bigger way than ever. His work has long encompassed scenography and ephemeral installations, among them crowd-pleasing turns at AD Intérieurs, the erstwhile annual showcase hosted by AD France.

In the formal salon, a pair of carved wood armchairs with inlaid stone backs have seat cushions of a Dedar fabric. Darré-designed objects include his Calder table, Minos rug, and Lyre mirror. He also created the trompe-l’oeil pilasters topped with 18th-century gilded wooden capitals. Late-19th-century French lantern; 1940s Italian ceramic dolphin table.

In the guest bedroom, Darré sits on an 18th-century gilded wood bench upholstered in velvet by Métaphores. A Darré-painted mural frames the 18th century Italian headboard upholstered in Tony Duquette’s Xanadu fabric for Jim Thompson. The bedcover and cushions are from Darré’s collection for Monoprix.

It has been revealed that darré was born in Paris, in the 14th, and went to school there as a boy. When his parents separated in the 1970s, his father—a sociologist—moved to the Luberon, and Vincent went with him; not long after, his mother, unwilling to live far from her son, also moved south, to Montpellier. “This allowed me to be Parisian, but also one who knew other places,” he states. It’s a telling detail: the South of France has informed his eye ever since, with its particular sense of light, water, and ease. Though he first went to school for fashion, his real love was drawing, as it had been since childhood. “Sometimes people are surprised,” he notes, “that a finished work of mine is almost always exactly like I had drawn it.”.

After a series of Paris apartments over the years, Darré has recently acquired a getaway in Toulon, the Mediterranean port city. The attraction was immediate. He had been invited to preside over the jury of Design Parade, the summer design festival held in Toulon and Hyères, and the city seized him the moment he arrived. “Once I got to the airport, in 2017, I immediately felt I was home. Chez moi! I had never experienced that feeling before.” He kept an eye on the listings and, after a few false starts, found exactly what he wanted.

In the entrance, Darré’s Vase Soleil stands atop a 1940s Venetian console table against a wall decorated with trompe l’oeil caryatids.

A 19th-century rattan sofa upholstered in Jean Lurçat’s Sirenes fabric by Pierre Frey.

Overlooking the Toulon harbor, the primary bedroom’s office area features several Darré designs including his Orphée sconce, Singez-moi table lamp, the carved and lacquered wood desk, a Vertebré chair cushioned in a fabric by Pierre Le-Tan, and a Column stool.

It has been revealed that lion head mascarons flank the doorway into the primary bedroom. 1970s plaster Buddha lamps with Darré-painted shades stand atop 17th-century French consoles. A 1960s plaster seahorse is displayed in the fireplace.

Recent findings suggest that the apartment occupies the top floor of a little three-story house overlooking the fishing port—a compact 860 square feet with stunning views of the sea. It was already lovely when he moved in, all white, with nothing architectural to be done: the perfect backdrop for Darré and his pencils and paints. He brought many of his favorite things—collections, objects, and furniture gathered over the years, added to since at the Drouot auction house and the little brocantes he loves to haunt. Furnishing was, he says, a gradual process, bringing in pieces little by little and slowly making the space his own over time.

According to recent reports, darré’s Crocodile bench stands in the primary bedroom. Two-Faced lamps with hand-painted shades atop Pas Gigogne tables flank the bed, and his Poisson bookcase is at left. The plaster chandelier is by Mathieu Challières, and the plaster unicorns are from a set designed by Jean Cocteau.

A metal figure given to Darré by Ines de la Fressange stands next to his Singez-moi lamp on the office area desk.

Darré’s Tabou shelf in the primary bedroom.

The exterior of the harbor-front house.

Darré on his Column stool with a 19th-century gilt-wood mirror from a Paris flea market.

In a recent development, darré speaks often of his love for Toulon, and of Jean Cocteau, who adored this coast and painted frescoes nearby. “I like the sweetness of life here,” he says. “Nothing has really changed since the 1950s. It’s the Provence of another era.” Every little square has its fountain; everyone is kind. It’s a military port, but its douceur de vie is what holds him.

The apartment represents Vincent Darré to a T: not an unadorned surface in sight, a home full of memories, tributes, and joy. “This has been one of my dreams, to have a house on the water,” he notes. “My place in Paris is exactly the same, though not on the water. But both are little suspended palaces. I create my own follies.” From the painted columns flanking the windows—among his very first purchases, which have followed him from home to home—to the mermaids and sea creatures and the tented bed, everything belongs to the fantastical world of Darré. As one of his teachers observed early on, you could recognize his hand from the very start.

A close-up of Darré’s ceramic Two-Faced lamp.

The dining area features a red lacquer table and chairs with Darré’s Dolphin lamp in the corner.

That world is entirely his own. He draws on a lineage of great fantasists—Charles de Beistegui, Henri Samuel, Jean Cocteau, Christian Bérard, Tony Duquette—yet the result, for all its jumble, is rigorously coherent. His flourish is always present. As the actress Isabelle Adjani once told him, to enter one of his interiors is to step into one of his drawings. Which is exactly what he wants.

Industry observers note that for all the bounce in his step, Darré is no one’s fool. He knows we live in difficult times, and likes the idea of adding a flourish of fantasy to reality. “I have my little world—a dream universe, but one you can live in.” He loves to dance, and even took tap-dancing lessons as a teenager, all the better to channel Fred Astaire or Gene Kelly. “Life is a film, and we are the actors,” he says. “That’s why I always dress the way I do.” Lights, camera, action—Darré is always ready.

Bitcoin Price Slips to Lows Not Seen Since 2024, Nasdaq Plunges 5%

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price slid to near $58,300 on Friday afternoon, down about 6.2% over the past 24 hours, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a deepening selloff in chip and artificial intelligence stocks sent the Nasdaq down about 5% and pushed bitcoin just under its summer low.
  • Bitcoin broke below $60,000 late Friday morning, a few hours after this morning’s report had it near $61,500.
  • Selling on Wall Street sped up through the afternoon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price slid to near $58,300 on Friday afternoon, down about 6.2% over the past 24 hours, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a deepening selloff in chip and artificial intelligence stocks sent the Nasdaq down about 5% and pushed bitcoin just under its summer low.

Bitcoin broke below $60,000 late Friday morning, a few hours after this morning’s report had it near $61,500. Over the past 24 hours, the bitcoin price has traded between $57,655 and $62,562, a drop of about $3,880. Bitcoin is down about 25% in November, on pace for its worst month since June 2022.

Selling on Wall Street sped up through the afternoon. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5% in late trading and the S&P 500 dropped about 3.5%. Yahoo Finance said the Nasdaq was on pace to close negative for the year, while the S&P 500 was poised to close in correction territory.

According to recent reports, chipmakers led the drop. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 12.5% to near $128, and AMD, Broadcom and Micron also posted double-digit losses. Gold futures dropped nearly 5%. Treasury yields fell as traders rotated into bonds and defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare, Reuters reported.

It has been revealed that anthropic (ANT) fell nearly 12% to around $86 on its first full day of trading, leaving it just above its $83 IPO price. The stock had closed its Thursday debut at $97.17 after raising $81.3 billion in the largest IPO of all time, CNBC reported.

It has been revealed that leveraged traders were forced out as the bitcoin price broke support. About $1.53 billion in crypto bets were wiped out over 24 hours, with long positions making up $1.4 billion of that total. Bitcoin alone accounted for around $540 million, while ether fell more than 8% to around $1,600.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin funds have been sellers, too. Investors have pulled roughly $3.5 billion from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs so far this month, including $582 million on Thursday. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest one-day outflow on record.

Recent findings suggest that rate worries are adding pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a half-point Federal Reserve hike in December. Traders still saw a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point increase, and some strategists warned that further hikes could deepen the selloff.

According to recent reports, coinShares head of research James Butterfill stated the drop looks driven more by the AI stock selloff than by problems inside crypto. Bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other growth assets that depend on easy money, he said.

The dip to $57,655 briefly took bitcoin just under its summer low near $57,700. It is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest losing streak since 2022.

Strategy (MSTR) fell about 8.4% to near $78.90, adding to the losses after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) dropped about 5.5% to near $103. Robinhood (HOOD) lost about 9.6% and Circle (CRCL) fell about 7.9%.

Bitcoin miners fared worst. MARA Holdings (MARA) sank about 17% to near $5.17, IREN (IREN) fell about 17% and CleanSpark (CLSK) dropped about 16%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 8.4%, and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) fell about 9.4%. Many miners have expanded into AI data centers, tying their shares to the chip selloff.

The bitcoin price is now down more than 50% from its record above $126,000, set in October 2025.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $58,300.

Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.
  • It has been revealed that “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP).
  • Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that “We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, noted in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.".

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

According to recent reports, that said, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

Industry observers note that although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

It has been revealed that “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some customers might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

Bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That said, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

In a recent development, “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very massive signatures,” he mentioned. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

According to recent reports, whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

According to recent reports, andré Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#133013. Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever.
  • While calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a.
  • “I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever. My thoughts were racing, and even for someone who deals with her share of anxiety, I was way beyond my normal self. So, I did what any person would do in that moment: I called my sister.

While calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a. one of the leading psychiatric institutions in the whole country, so let’s just say she knows how to handle an anxious person. Her suggestion was to go to the kitchen, grab a major bowl, fill it with ice water, and then dunk my face in it. I wasn’t exactly thrilled by the idea. It seemed like a whole bunch of work for something that couldn’t possibly help me in such a state.

“I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she stated. She could tell I thought the idea was silly, and that I was probably going to skip it. And, I did think it was silly, but she seemed weirdly passionate that I submerge my face into a bowl of freezing water, so I complied. I grabbed a bowl, filled it with water and ice cubes, and reluctantly got my face wet, just barely making sure my nose and eyes were underwater.

According to recent reports, I felt better basically instantly. The racing thoughts subsided and I could finally see straight. Even more impressive is the fact that once I reentered the situation that was making me anxious, all that nervous energy simply didn’t return. I was reset and relaxed. All it took was a bucket of water and about 30 seconds.

The trick—or, skill, I should say—that my sister taught me comes from dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), a modality that was created by Marsha Linehan, PhD, who recently passed away at 83 years old. It was a breakthrough treatment for people facing extreme mental health challenges like chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder, which Linehan revealed she struggled with in 2011, decades after DBT became the gold standard for treating those conditions.

Recent findings suggest that whether or not you are someone who deals with a formal mental health diagnosis or the occasional tough moment, DBT skills can make a significant difference. The cold water trick my sister taught me is called an “ice dive,” and it’s one of four simple DBT tools that can help snap you out of a range of intense emotions quickly. Now, any time I feel myself getting heightened, my immediate next thought is: I should go grab a bucket of ice water. Call me converted.

Here’s how you can practice this skill too, plus, the three others that work just as well—and don’t involve water.

Meet the experts: Shireen Rizvi, PhD, is a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in New York City. Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, is a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic.

At this point, you’ve pretty much gotten the entire gist of an ice dive, but let’s recap: All it takes is a bowl significant enough to get your full face in and some chilly water. (The colder the better, but it doesn’t need to reach ice bath territory.) Once you’ve got that, place it on a low-set table or even on the ground—you want to be bending over when you dunk your head in to mimic something closer to a dive—take a deep breath, and submerge your face, especially around your nasal passages and eyes, for as long as possible. 30 seconds is ideal, but that may feel like a really long time at first. Just go for as long as you can, and feel free to repeat multiple times for a cumulative total of 30 seconds.

As for what is going on when you do this: Dunking your face in cold water triggers what is called the mammalian dive reflex, claims Shireen Rizvi, PhD, a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in Newly introduced York City. “It’s automatic,” she says. “You’re not doing anything consciously to create the reaction, which is there to help mammals survive cold water.”.

Sources indicate that an ice dive triggers a survival mode where our bodies reduce our heart rate, slow down our breathing, and redirect blood to our vital organs, she explains. Under water, it helps you stay alive, but on land, it helps calm just about any activating emotion you might be experiencing. And, your face being what’s submerged is critical to get this specific reaction; getting in an ice bath where your face isn’t underwater actually spikes your heart rate due to cold shock, for example.

Basically, an ice dive forces your body to focus on the bare necessities, like staying calm. It’s best used anytime your emotions are reaching a 90-plus on a scale of 1 to 100, Rizvi says, whether the emotion is anxiety, anger, stress, jealousy, or anything else. If you’re feeling it intensely and your heart rate is up, an ice dive can help.

Industry observers note that there’s one other handy use case too: If you’re ruminating. “When your body is in a survival mode, it's pulling resources back, and it actually also pulls your attention too, so if you have a lot of thoughts floating around in your head making you anxious, this can also help clear your mind temporarily,” says Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic. Think of it this way: “You can't be thinking about a grocery list if you have just fallen into ice water,” she says.

And, while this trick has completely changed the game for me, I have some good news: There are three others that all have the same effect sans H2O.

An ice dive makes up the very first letter—T for temperature—in the TIPP acronym, which is a part of DBT’s distress tolerance pillar. The rest (intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation) can all quickly calm and reset your nervous system, no liquid necessary.

All four skills have a similar basic mechanism. They take you from a heightened state (or a distressed one, to use DBT-speak) where your sympathetic nervous system is activated and bring you back into a relaxed one, where your parasympathetic nervous system is in the driver’s seat again. They’re not about talking or reflecting; they’re about helping you feel better in a moment when emotions are extreme.

“These are skills that act to regulate your physiology,” Cox indicates. “Oftentimes when you are having an intense emotion, you think you have to handle it with your mind. These are skills that help you handle it with your body.” Of course, once you’re out of that intense moment, you may want to call on other mental tools and process what happened—but that’s not where you’re at when you’re calling on a TIPP skill. They’re for when you’re in crisis mode.

You can use any of them at any time with one crucial caveat: All TIPP skills are meant to rapidly slow down your heart rate, so if you’re someone with a heart condition or who takes meds like beta blockers, talk to your doctor first before trying any of them, Rizvi says.

Without further ado, here’s what you need to know about the other three skills.

In a recent development, the I in TIPP stands for intense exercise. This may sound similarly prohibitive to needing a bowl of water, but it’s actually quite simple. All you really need to do is get moving for about 30 seconds. Do some all-out jumping jacks, pump your arms up and down as fast as you can while sitting in your chair, or get into a plank. Just get your heart rate up and your muscles feel fatigued. “It feels paradoxical, but when you end that short burst of exercise, everything slows down,” Rizvi indicates.

There’s also an added benefit to going with exercise. When you’re feeling a heightened emotion, one of the ways your sympathetic nervous system reacts is by sending out glucose into your bloodstream, Cox notes. Again, this is an automatic, physical reaction, and it’s what gives you the energy for either a fight or flight response. But since you're probably not feeling anxious or angry because you need to escape a pack of hungry wolves, you probably won’t end up literally running away or fighting them off and using that energy. Exercising eats up some of that extra glucose, helping you get back to baseline.

If you’ve ever done box breathing, you’ve done the first P in TIPP. All it involves is breathing in and out in a controlled manner for a set number of seconds each time. “The main core of this technique is that your out breath needs to be longer than your in breath,” claims Cox. “That is what activates your parasympathetic nervous system and slows everything down.”.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to keeping your out breath longer than your in breath (say four seconds in and eight out), you also want to make sure you’re breathing from your diaphragm, Rizvi says. You can monitor this by placing your hand on your belly. If it’s rising and falling with each breath, you’re breathing from your diaphragm.

If you’re looking for an entry-level DBT skill, or one that you can do in pretty much any context, this is a good one to master. “I find paced breathing in particular is something that you can usually do no matter where you are or what you're doing,” Rizvi says. It takes no setup, no resources, and you can even do it in plain sight without people noticing.

In a recent development, finally, the last TIPP skill is paired muscle relaxation. “When we are having an intense emotion, our body tenses up,” Cox says. “This helps release some of that tension.”.

Recent findings suggest that to do this skill, start at one end of your body and systematically work your way up or down, tensing and releasing your muscles throughout and saying the word “relax” each time. Pairing the muscle tensing with the word relax also helps train them—and therefore you—to relax on command, Cox says.

There are plenty of guided paired muscle relaxation routines you can follow online, but you can also just do it on your own, tensing as many muscle groups as you’d like (or have time for).

Sources indicate that don’t have time to reread an article in a moment of crisis? Here are the quick and simple basics of all the TIPP skills for when you need to use them ASAP.

Recent findings suggest that no matter which one you go for, remember this: “Emotions fire in the order of milliseconds,” Cox states. That means that no matter how intense the thing you’re feeling is, it will pass, and probably much faster than you think. Sometimes, all our brains need is a reset initiated by our bodies.

My interest in hair removal started in elementary school when I snuck into my mom's medicine cabinet and dragged her razor across my leg like I was coloring with my favorite box of markers. Needless to say, I've learned the right way to shave since then (namely to apply shaving cream and gently glide my razor toward the grain with light pressure).

I've had a lot of help perfecting my technique—as a beauty editor with a decade of testing experience, I have access to the best dermatologists and aestheticians. Yet, no matter how on-point my upcoming shaving technique is now, most women's razors never get my legs quite as smooth. And other hair removal methods are super painful, ripping strands out at the root. Ouch!

But then, I upgraded to electric razors—and I've never turned back.

“A closer shave can feel nice, but because the surface of our skin is not perfectly smooth, it inevitably results in removal of some skin cells,” indicates dermatologist Caroline Robinson, MD. This can lead to microscopic nicks and irritation. “Electric razors can help avoid this. They’re typically less sensitizing,” says Dr. Robinson, because the shave they provide is not as close. At-home laser hair removal devices, waxing, sugaring, and threading are all great options for hair removal if you’ve got the time (and the coin), but if silky-smooth skin sans irritation is what you’re after, the answer is electric.

Sources indicate that over the past two years, Women's Health editors have been testing popular electric razors to determine which seven are worth the investment. Ultimately, we found that the Philips Beauty Series was the best multi-use product due to its five-blade razor and dual-sidedness that allows for a super close shave. Meanwhile, the Remington Smooth & Silky On-the-Go Shaver delivers on quality for quick touch-ups while being budget- and travel-friendly. Read on to see our other winners from our testing process.

Sources indicate that A favorite of our editors, this hair removal device hits all of the targets we're looking for when buying an electric razor. For starters, it literally has 40 micro-grip tweezers in its motor to provide a super close shave, keeping your skin smooth for weeks at a time. While that might seem intimidating, it upgrades your in-shower shaving routine in a major way.

You can hit even the trickiest spots on your body. From your underarms and belly down to your ankles, this electric razor has you covered quite literally from head to toe. And with an impressive 50-minute runtime you can eliminate all of my unwanted hair with this device at least a couple of times before recharging it for just an hour. You’ll also appreciate that it's lightweight but not flimsy like it'll slip out of your grip. Plus, it's waterproof so you can shave in the shower without worrying about your fresh razor cranking out mid-shave.

An upgrade from the original Braun model, the more expensive but higher-tech Flex comes with a flexible head (hence, the name) that can uniquely adapt to your body's curves and contours—even the complicated corners of your bikini line. In addition to the epilator, the bundle also comes with a body exfoliation brush, skin contact cap for additional comfort, and more—definitely a bargain.

"The face and body brushes are especially useful, and I love how you can interchange the heads depending on what type of cleansing you want to do," claims Women's Health contributor Isabel McMahon.

She credits the device’s built-in light, called the "smartlight," as a great option for women who like dimmer lighting while showering but still want to see what they're doing.

Read more: Best At-Home Laser Hair Removal Devices.

Industry observers note that we previously tried and enjoyed the Philips Lady Shaver Series 6000, but it's no longer available. Thankfully, the brand upgraded to the 9000 model—and we love the changes.

Sources indicate that you're paying $30 more, but it's worth the upgrade. The new model is a more powerful device that has two speed settings for faster plucking. It also features a quicker two-hour recharge time and can be used cordless for up to an hour.

The 9000 is equipped with eight attachments, including a floating foil head that glides across the skin. The different blades of the Philips electric razor are designed to target specific areas of your body, like the more compact bikini trimmer comb and head versus the larger trimming comb for your legs. It does an excellent job of trimming coarse body hair without any irritation or tugging.

Regardless of which attachment you employ, they all ensure that you can shave safely, even in the tightest contours of your legs and underarms. Whether you shave wet or dry, the ergonomic handle design will make sure nothing slips through your fingers. For this reason, we think the Philips is an incredible value. There are other, less expensive options on our list, but they're not quite as versatile in terms of where you can use them, so that's why this one took the top value spot.

Looking to stay silky-smooth on vacay? Then click “add to cart” on this extremely travel-friendly razor and then toss it in your carry-on or gym bag for quick, simple touch-ups. It's compact, so it won't take up precious room in your cosmetic bag (you could even stash it in your office drawer to ensure that you're hair-free for any impromptu after-work activities like happy hours and date nights). And yep, this little shaver is super lightweight to carry which is always a win.

Despite being battery-powered, you'll be shocked by how durable it is compared to something cheaper. This dual trimmer lifts and guides the blades for smooth results whether you're shaving wet or dry. It does a great job for the price, but you might notice that it seems to work best when the hair is longer, so it may not be ideal for targeting stubble. (It's totally NBD, though, because you can just shave less often and ultimately who doesn't love that?).

Industry observers note that it's also not waterproof or durable for daily, consistent use so you wouldn't want to consider this your primary hair remover, but for a quick trip—brilliant! No wonder it earned an impressive 4.1-star average from more than 14,430 Amazon reviews.

Our favorite Philips model is no longer being sold, but we found a much cheaper alternative that doesn’t skimp on quality. After all, it can be nerve-racking to take an epilator or electric razor to the face, but this compact model was made just for that.

Recent findings suggest that it’s shaped like a lipstick tube and features a hypoallergenic head that glides over rogue chin hairs and your upper lip with ease. Though it lacks a built-in mirror or LED light so you can conveniently see and remove even the smallest facial hairs, this device is only $20 compared to the $47 Philips model. With those savings you could easily treat yourself to a light up makeup to ensure you see every unwanted hair.

"I love this face shaver when I'm having one of those all-out spa nights," says Wohlner. She notes that, when paired with a liquid exfoliant and a hydrating face mask, the results are truly out of this world.

Sources indicate that pro tip: You should try using it before your skincare routine to help your products to really penetrate the skin for a major glow. Just don't use anything with too many active ingredients like retinol right after as that can cause sensitivity.

Industry observers note that amazon reviewers can’t get enough of this affordable electric razor. It boasts a casual 4.2-star average from nearly 15,500 Amazon reviews. No wonder it earned the top spot as Amazon’s number one bestselling electric razor. So what makes it so effective for you? It does a little bit of everything well! There are five interchangeable heads that target everything from the bikini area and legs to underarms and face. If you’re dealing with rogue hairs in hard-to-reach areas, use this one for touchups. It comes with trimmers and traditional razor heads so you can snip longer hairs to about the length of a rice grain before shaving. Offering IPX7 waterproof protection, you can confidently shave in the shower with this device or use it dry if you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that this Philips electric razor has a large head and self-sharpening blade to rapidly remove facial hair. Wohlner considers this tool as the most effective method for eliminating stubborn upper lip and chin hairs. "While it's too substantial to remove hair on my brows, it's awesome for those larger areas of the face when you're short on time and want to look smooth and stubble-free," she indicates.

According to recent reports, this shaver has a hypoallergenic stainless steel head that doesn’t irritate sensitive skin, quickly removing unwanted hair in a single pass without causing pain or discomfort. The Series 5000 keeps Wohlner's face smooth, and it always glides over the skin effortlessly without leaving it red and raw. It even comes with a built-in mirror in the cap to touch-up on the go.

In a recent development, pro tip: The large shaver head does tend to get clogged after a few uses, which can be prevented if you wipe it down with alcohol after every use. Taking care of your device will ensure you get the closest shave and that it lasts for years.

This razor, which is specifically designed for the bikini and underarm areas, can be used both inside and outside the shower, no matter your hair type. It's ideal for thick, coarser hair, though, because it has a sharp blade that trims them on the first attempt. Additionally, this cordless device has rounded edges to prevent accidents. Anyone who's shaved knows hair removal can get messy, but the head on this shaver opens up for easy rinsing, too.

You’ll appreciate how beginner-friendly the Philips razor is. The instructions are so clear and easy to follow, which make your experience a breeze. The electric razor is relatively small and very easy to get a secure grip on, so anyone with butterfingers can rely on this device.I tried this razor and think it's pretty sweet, especially when cleaning up my bikini line. At first I was nervous that my longer hairs would get caught in the razor (it was winter, please let me live), but I was pleasantly surprised that it was a nonissue. It actually gets down quite low, especially when I don't use the comb attachment.

I enjoyed my bikini line shaving experience enough to use this device on my underarms and that's when I realized it heats up relatively rapidly, which may be something to keep in mind if you're going for a longer shave sesh. Unlike the sold out Gillette razor we featured, Philips is rechargeable, so you won’t have to buy batteries once it dies out.

With the multitude of options available on Amazon, Ulta, and Dermstore, there are a couple of features to consider the next time you're in the market for a fresh shave:.

Industry observers note that more is not always better. In fact, a larger number of blades can sometimes increase irritation, says dermatologist Lauren Ploch, MD. On the other hand, fewer blades mean more passes over the skin, which can also cause irritation. It's about finding a happy medium that works for you. This may take some testing, so remember to try out your razor on a small patch of skin to see how you react before going all in.

According to recent reports, think about how well a razor feels and fits in your hand. You want something that’s well-balanced and not too heavy for the most comfortable shaving experience. Also consider if it will shave wet or dry. Not all electric razors can be used in the shower, Dr. Ploch points out. So, if you're a shower shaver, make sure to grab something waterproof and cordless.

Sources indicate that you also want to make sure your razor head can contour to your body's curves, especially when you're targeting areas like the bikini line, underarms, toes, and even legs. Some of the razors on this list, like the Panasonic Close Curves Electric Razor, can uniquely adapt to the body's curves with their rotating heads.

If a razor is rechargeable (big plus already), make sure to check how long it takes to charge and the battery life. If you don't want to deal with a cord or annoying charge time, some of the options on this list—hi, Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover—are battery-powered, which may be more convenient while traveling.

Some razors come with trimmers, blade guides, and changeable blade heads for different areas of the body. If you're looking for more of a Swiss Army knife-type, multi-tool situation, take a look at the available attachments. Then, see if those are compatible with the parts of your body you want to tackle.

According to recent reports, believe it or not, many razors have a warranty, so if you're unsatisfied with your purchase, you can most likely return it for a longer period than you might think. Most razors on this list have a 30-day warranty, which gives you ample time for testing.

Our team tests a wide range of products and services to provide our readers with reliable, honest, and trustworthy information. It's our belief that our readers deserve the best, which is why our recommendations have been thoroughly tested and vetted by our very own editors. For the past year, Women’s Health editors, including myself, and contributors Jasmine Gomez and Sabrina Talbert, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated electric razors. Our team also consulted four dermatologists, and then evaluated thousands of customer reviews and ratings to narrow down the seven best electric razors for a wide range of needs and preferences.

Ready for smooth, bump-free skin? Look no further than these editor-tested and expert-approved electric razors for women, below.

In a recent development, if you struggle with bumps and irritation, an electric razor might be your fresh best friend. Of course, you still need to make sure you use that electric razor properly. Dermatologists say you should follow the below best practices for a smooth shave every time.

Make sure your skin is well hydrated before shaving because using an electric razor over dry, irritated skin can make matters worse, states dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD. Dr. Robinson adds that you should also use a gentle cleanser prior to shaving. And, avoid fragrance or products known to cause irritation immediately before and after shaving, she says.

And please, do so in the direction of the hair growth, says Dr. Zeichner. Repeated strokes over the same area increase the likelihood of irritation and ingrown hairs.

Recent findings suggest that hydration is key. "I advise patients that they do not need a dedicated post-shave or aftercare lotion—a gentle moisturizer is just fine in these areas," says Dr. Robinson, who likes light, fragrance-free formulas. Aside from that, Dr. Robinson recommends making sure you follow any specific instructions on the product package—in other words, you should actually read the directions.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, everyone's going to have their personal preference, and it's not worth, ahem, splitting hairs if you prefer one type of razor over another. That being mentioned, if your skin is prone to irritation, it might be time to ditch the traditional razor. With an electric razor, you’re not scraping against the skin really hard like a traditional razor does, states dermatologist Cameron Rokhsar, MD. This means that you won't see a lot of the cuts and burns that sometimes result from a manual blade, says Dr. Rokhsar. There are also areas of the body that might be better suited to shave with an electric razor. "Most women's electric razors are designed for our curvy areas," says Dr. Ploch. "I prefer electric razors around the ankles because manual razors cut this area easily.".

Sources indicate that keeping your electric razor clean is incredibly important, states Dr. Rokhsar. Many derms will recommend changing a manual razor every time you shave, but you can't do that with an electric one, which makes running the blades under warm water after use a crucial step. This will keep it free of hair, shaving cream, and other residues.

Dr. Rokhsar also recommends swiping over the blades and the outside of the razor with a rubbing alcohol-soaked cotton ball regularly. "Especially if it sits in your bathroom moisture, bacteria will accumulate on the blades," he says. "It's an easy entry point for bacteria to go down the hair follicle." That's a major no-no if you want to stay free of irritation or infection.

According to recent reports, our team of editors follow Dr. Rokhsar's advice and it hasn't led us astray. And despite evaluating some of these razors for close to a year, we are pleased that we haven't noticed any rusting after using the alcohol-soaked cotton ball.

Recent findings suggest that another tip is to actually read and follow the maintenance instructions of your device. (Admittedly, we threw ours away since we've been using these for several months and like to keep the limited space of our beauty closet as streamlined as possible.) You can also prioritize using devices like the Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover that's easy to clean, as the head can easily be removed so you can dump shaved hair and dead skin cells straight into the garbage.

It has been revealed that THE MOST CONVENIENT travel companion is a backpack, and I envy those who can pack a trip’s worth of clothing into one. But I need a carry-on suitcase; I like to think of it as option packing instead of overpacking. For years I relied on my Filson Duffle—and still love it as a weekender—but found myself wanting a roller bag for hands-free travel and to get a little more organization.

According to recent reports, carry-on suitcases are quite bland though. They’re plastic boxes that require you to attach a keychain or bandana just to recognize your own. I considered Rimowa’s iconic carry-ons for a short while until I remembered my tax bracket and came back to reality (if you’re unfamiliar, they’re expensive). More palatable aluminum options from Away and Monos exist, but they miss the mark for me, be it style or features.

Recent findings suggest that A lucky typo while searching Porter Yoshida bags led me to Portar luggage. The brand’s aluminum and polycarbonate/aluminum luggage is sleek, durable, and costs a fifth of a Rimowa cabin bag. I used the Portar Aluminum Carry-On Luggage all summer and it exceeded my expectations, and it’s now seeing me through holiday travel.

It has been revealed that portar’s carry-on is exactly what I was looking for lookswise—an unbranded aluminum suitcase with leather handles. Functionally, it surpassed expectations after trips to Michigan, Chicago, Houston, and Amsterdam.

Industry observers note that the aluminum shell has held up to TSA's less-than-careful hands over the past couple of months. Aluminum luggage gathers minor dings and scuffs throughout travel—it’s part of the charm—but the black covers any marks I may have picked up, and I don’t notice any. I also like the rivets along the shell's border. It reminds me of old travel trunks I’ve seen in vintage stores.

The leather handles are not only a nice aesthetic touch, but they actually make handling the suitcase much easier. They’re substantial and padded, unlike the flimsy plastic strip you see on a lot of carry-on luggage. It makes hoisting it into the overhead cabin a bit more steady and secure.

Recent findings suggest that the latches are also a huge change for me, as I’m used to hassling with zippers that snag or tear—I will never go back to zippered luggage again. Both the telescopic handle and wheels operate smoothly, so I glide gracefully to my gate.

Industry observers note that technically my fiancée’s Away carry-on has more space based on dimensions, but I swear I can efficiently pack more into my Portar. Maybe it’s the clever pocket configuration or the removable compression straps and divider, but coming back from Amsterdam, we were counting on my Portar to bring back Delft ceramics and other acquisitions. All of which fit despite my over (option!) packing.

In a recent development, my Portar will now accompany me home for the holidays. It will also travel to the Pitztal Valley in Austria, then on to Vienna the week after Thanksgiving. It’s a first-class carry-on in the cabin space above my economy seat. Air travel used to be luxurious, and people would dress up for the occasion of reaching 38,000 feet. The Portar carry-on is bringing back some of that charm and costs me less than $300.

Bonus: a hidden waistband pocket makes it easy to stash small essentials on the go. As a runner myself, I’ve found them perfect for carrying keys during jogs—they always stay in place.

While they’re budget-friendly, these aren’t the most durable leggings we’ve tested. If you’re looking for a pair for intense workouts, we’d steer you elsewhere. But for staying cool, comfy, and sweat-free on travel days, Helms can’t recommend these enough.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot to love about these leggings, but I’m a huge fan of the high, compressive waistband. It hits just above the belly button and applies just enough compression to keep my core feeling locked in without feeling too tight or falling down mid-workout. Plus, the compression holds up through everything from weightlifting to yoga, and the high-waisted fit is both flattering and comfortable. I also love the smooth, flat seams, which help prevent chafing, and the contoured stitching on the back that helps flatter the bum. Helms wears these weekly and swears by the cooling fabric. The quick-drying material keeps sweat from lingering, so if you’re heading to the store post-gym, you won’t feel gross in the checkout line.

While we wish this legging came in more colors, the true-to-size, flattering, and comfortable fit still makes this pair one of our faves.

We also love that the brand offers a range of designs, from pocketed options to classic, streamlined pairs. It’s available in three lengths, so there’s a pair for every height. Sources indicate that if you’re on a budget, it doesn’t get better than this three-pack of leggings for under $30 (yep, really). The best part? The low price doesn’t mean you’re sacrificing quality. These are actually some of Amazon’s top-rated leggings, and for good reason.

Sources indicate that editors who tested this pocketed trio say they’re soft yet supportive, holding up well through deep squats and mobility work. They also offer standout tummy control, making them a solid pick if you’re after a slimming fit.

Industry observers note that another bonus: there are no front or inner thigh seams, so you won’t get any extra bulk or uncomfortable rubbing. The only downside? The fabric is a bit on the thinner side, so you’ll want to be careful while washing to avoid pilling.

It has been revealed that unlike other plus-size leggings our editors tested, this legging doesn’t dig in at the waist or roll down mid-workout. Plus, it’s made with flat-lock seams to help prevent chafing and irritation.

While it’s not the most technical pair (cotton isn’t moisture-wicking, and there are no pockets), it earns high marks for comfort, everyday wearability, and price.

Looking for a cropped legging for summer or warmer workouts? I recommend this chafe-proof, squat-proof, and sweat-wicking pair. Recent findings suggest that while the seams and waistband lie flat, we did notice that the side pockets stick out slightly and add a bit of width to the legs. That said, the hidden interior pocket at the waistband is a major win for securely stashing small items at the gym. Plus, the waistband features built-in tummy control that holds you in and adds a smooth, toned look while you work out.

Women’s Health executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos swears by this high-waisted, budget-friendly pair. “I love a high-waisted legging with pockets for my phone and credit card, so I can really go hands-free when I walk and run,” she states.

She wears them for everything: from running and weight-lifting to travel days and lounging at home. The fabric is smooth and substantial, yet still super breathable. “They feel more expensive than they are,” she adds, noting that she owns “way too many” pairs.

Sources indicate that during testing, we did notice that the waistband can roll down slightly, and we wish there were more inseam options beyond the standard 25 inches. But for the price, comfort, and versatility, this pair is tough to beat.

According to recent reports, need a lil ~flare~ in your life? Check out this Topyogas legging. We love this pair because it’s just as flattering as it is versatile. Pair this pant with a T-shirt and blazer for work, and nobody will know you're the comfiest person in the office (then, head straight to yoga after happy hour).

When we put them to the test at the gym, we really appreciated the moisture-wicking material. Even after a hot yoga class, I felt way drier than I was expecting.

It has been revealed that after testing this legging, we agree that their softness is top-notch. Plus, the high-rise fit offers just enough tummy control, so we can confidently wear it with just a high-impact sports bra or a crop top. The V-shaped waist is also super flattering, giving the appearance of a slightly longer torso. That being noted, there is a bit of extra fabric around the crotch, which is supposed to give that area more breathing room, but might be too baggy for some wearers.

Women's Health food producer Tina Martinez touts these Hey Nuts leggings for their smooth, light feel and ability to stay in place. She loves that they offer ample support, and that they feel like they're holding you in the right places. Martinez also loves their great compression, the fact that they don't roll down, and how opaque they are (no panty lines here!). They're also super stretchy and comfortable, so you can wear them at home or to the gym.

Industry observers note that these leggings have the most inseam options on this list, ranging from 25 inches to 31 inches if you're on the taller side. In terms of sizing, our testers find that these leggings run totally true-to-size, which, if you're an avid Amazon shopper, you know is hard to come by.

We had very few cons about these leggings, but we did agree that the butt seam felt a bit too low, so they're not the most flattering option on this list.

According to recent reports, professor Preeti Arya, PhD, specializes in textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology. She states that the right fabric for leggings depends on your needs. But if you're worried about maintenance, "you can go for something that is petroleum-based because care is easy," she says. Petroleum-based fabrics include spandex, polyester, and nylon. These options are also typically much cheaper, according to Arya, but you can also opt for wool or silk, which sometimes feel better on your skin since they're natural fibers. Heads up: these fabrics are a bit harder to care for, though, and require special attention on laundry day.

It has been revealed that rise is really up to your personal preference, but higher-rise leggings usually have tummy control, which is a plus when you want to feel snatched at the gym. However, tummy control typically comes with a bit more compression, which may not be great for lower-impact activities like yoga or casual walks.

It has been revealed that again, length is up to your personal preference, but the most flattering cut is typically just above your ankle. For most people, that means a 7/8 style of leggings. Full-length leggings, or ones that extend all the way to your feet, might be better for barefoot workouts like yoga. Other lengths, like capri leggings, are really up to your personal style.

To determine which leggings on Amazon are the best, we looked at factors including material options, the fit of each pair, price points that suit every budget, and what type of activity each legging is best suited to. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda’s automatic engine start-stop feature is under upcoming federal scrutiny, after the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration received hundreds of complaints that engines failed to restart automatically from a complete stop at a traffic light on certain models, prompting the agency to commence an investigation.

The federal probe, announced on Friday, November 13, includes 1.03 million units of the 2024-2026 Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline. The inquiry also includes 2024-2026 Acura MDX units. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation received 701 complaints related to the Auto Start/Stop feature.

“To help improve fuel efficiency, the Auto Start/Stop system will automatically shut off the engine when a vehicle comes to a complete stop. The engine is intended to automatically restart when a driver releases the brake pedal. However, the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system,” the investigation announcement reads.

It has been revealed that while automatic start-stop systems were created to improve fuel economy, Honda seems to be having a recurring concern with the feature. Federal safety regulators previously opened a probe into Honda’s automatic start-stop system in 2025. That investigation included 2.2 million late-model Honda Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, and Ridgeline models, as well as Acura MDX and TLX units. However, the new investigation includes 2026 model-year units. Inquiry documents allege that the two issue populations have different root causes and respond differently to repairs.

In a recent development, there have been no injuries related to this problem, according to the feds. EPA boss Lee Zeldin said the agency was investigating improvements or eliminating the technology last year; whether it sticks around in the long run, however, an engineering analysis of the stop-start system should bring Honda and NHTSA together to identify an effective solution to this recurring problem soon.

After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.
