The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get.
  • But then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get. Such as plentiful M branding everywhere. It was no surprise when I arrived at BMW’s proving ground in Miramar, France, to experience the M3 prototype for the first time to see numerous flags and banners with the famous slant “M” logo. And it felt equally natural for a moment to be listening to the sound of a hard-worked engine on the test track, with what seemed the entirely M-appropriate howl of a straight-six exhaling through a minimally muffled exhaust.

But then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted. Because it was an M4 GT4 making the compelling racket. The two M3 prototypes that followed it wearing a vibrant, dazzle pattern disguise, were traveling every bit as promptly but almost entirely silently.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock. The good news for anyone unsure about such a radical departure for the subbrand is that work on a gasoline-powered M3 is continuing in parallel. The combustion version, with the development code G85, is likely to feature another version of the S58 turbocharged inline-six from the current G80 generation, likely working in conjunction with some level of hybrid assistance. That will be a much more traditional take on the junior M car, but it almost certainly won’t be as powerful or as quick as the fully electric version.

But is our world ready for this level of different?

My first experience at Miramar was a passenger ride around the handling track, sitting in the left seat of one of the four colorfully-wrapped prototypes beside Sven Esch, M’s head of vehicle dynamics. I knew the car had a quad-motor powertrain, with one motor driving each wheel, and I could see it was riding on fresh Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires, but that was about all I had to go on when Esch executed a full launch-control start, one brutal enough to leave me confident the finished car will be another member of the two-second club when it comes to 0–60 times. The other disclosure, delivered from the changing tone of the noise coming from the speakers and the sight of Esch’s fingers working paddles behind the steering wheel, is that BMW is joining Hyundai, Porsche, and Mercedes in having a simulated gear system. The lap also revealed a handling balance familiar from many generations of M cars, with varying angles of oversteer through most of the corners.

There are still many unknowns. Although the cars at Miramar were close to production spec, BMW is keeping many details to itself. There are no performance claims yet. And every number given for power, torque, range and charging speed carried an asterisk leading to an “approximately” proviso. The maximum system output was quoted at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft, with the pair of front motors able to deliver up to 643 hp and 398 lb-ft working together, while the larger two in back max out at a claimed 750 hp and 738 lb-ft. Given the way automotive PR typically works, I would be surprised if any of those figures grew any worse before becoming finalized. But they are clearly a way off the 1153-hp AMG GT 63 4-Door, the 1123-hp Lucid Air Sapphire, and the 1019-hp Porsche Taycan Turbo GT.

Industry observers note that the M3 EV uses a different battery pack from the regular i3, with a newly introduced cell design and double-sided cooling to enable huge peak flow rates, with this having approximately 100 kWh of usable energy and operating at up to 800 volts. BMW is predicting an EPA range of 300 miles, and peak DC charging speeds will be around 420 kilowatts—slightly higher than the regular i3 and better than the speediest Taycan, but a way off the 600-kW capability of the AMG. More impressive is the ability of the battery pack to reabsorb energy through regeneration, doing this at rates of up to—approximately again—540 kilowatts. So the equivalent of 724 hp, without having to use the carbon-ceramic discs and pads.

Recent findings suggest that then there are the simulated gears. Although, pedantically, these are not. BMW has decided the mDrive mode allows the selection of what it calls “stages,” of which there are six. The default mode on startup is actually Automatic, in which the car changes between the stages by itself while playing a corresponding soundtrack as it does so, like a true automatic transmission in drive. There is also a paddle mode that gives you the ability to select a stage and also a simulated limiter if you fail to change up in time. It also has a normal EV single-speed drive mode.

It has been revealed that beneath the surface, the M3 has been given a substantial structural work over compared with the i3, the M version getting additional reinforcement for suspension subframes and also plates that bolt to the underfloor battery pack front and rear to better integrate this into the car’s structure. There is also a strut brace between the front suspension towers, eliminating the i3’s frunk, plus smaller reinforcement struts within the A-pillars and on the rear towers.

Industry observers note that while the M3 might be beaten by rivals on power statistics, it turns tables with the complexity of its powertrain. Having individual motors for each wheel is a segment first, in contrast with the two-motor Taycan Turbo GT and the three-motor AMG GT 4-Door and Lucid Air Sapphire. The lack of any physical connection between the different wheels means all the functions normally handled by differentials and clutch packs have to be done electronically, a hugely complex task for the dynamic control system. But it also brings benefits, most obvious is the ability to vary the torque going to each individual wheel almost instantly, without the response delay of even the fastest-acting mechanical systems. And it can also do this with regeneration, changing the braking effect on each wheel with equal dexterity.

According to recent reports, my chance to experience all this witchcraft was limited to two stints on the Miramar handling track, following the raucous M4 GTS being piloted by works driver Jens Klingmann at a pretty gentle pace, and with Carsten Wolf, vehicle characteristics manager, riding shotgun. Wolf proved to be a pretty laid-back passenger, but I was only able to switch certain dynamic settings.

While the electric M3’s cabin architecture is very similar to that of the i3 and the fresh 3-series, the prototype wore a dashboard cover to obscure what I’m told were unfinished screen-layout designs. The car did have an M-specific version of BMW’s Panoramic Vision extra-long gauge cluster, which features a rendered “rev counter” very similar in design to the one in the new M350 xDrive, two graphic bars moving apart. There was also a small set of color-changing shift lights.

In a recent development, it was immediately clear that performance was on another level to the i3 50 I had driven earlier the same day. The M3 felt every bit as quick as the power figures suggested it should, with none of the shortish straights of the handling track being long enough to bring any sense of acceleration beginning to tail off, even as speeds headed well north of 100 mph, and the M4 GT4 was visibly having to work hard to keep a gap. In a straightline fight, I’m certain the EV would have been the faster car, although riding on Pirelli slicks, and having Klingmann at the wheel, gave the car a clear advantage in corners.

Industry observers note that the M3’s steering was heavier than the i3 and M350’s and brought a far better sense of connection to the front tires. Unlike some cars with lots of electrical power going through the front axle, the prototype didn’t suffer from any steering corruption, albeit over what was generally a smooth track surface. Even in the softest Comfort mode, the car turned into corners with a keenness that was clearly being helped by applying different levels of regen to each wheel, which then kept it locked to a chosen line.

Or at least, it stayed locked until I started to try and get early onto the accelerator. At which point a newly introduced sensation arrived, unexpected in an M3: mild understeer. The control systems were clearly intervening hard in the background; winding off lock brought full fury back immediately. At Wolf’s suggestion, I pressed the steering wheel’s M1 button to shift the drivetrain and chassis to their Sport setting, reducing the front-end push.

But it required the M2 button, which brought the most aggressive Sport Plus settings, and putting the stability control into its half-off MDM mode to unlock the M3’s party spirit and show the side of its personality I’d first experienced from the passenger’s seat, with progressive, easily controllable oversteer.

In a recent development, plenty of magic was still going on behind the scenes. I noticed that even if I wasn’t quick to apply opposite lock, the prototype would still hold a tidy drift, the dynamic brain carefully metering the torque going to each corner—I was in no doubt that turning the stability management fully off would be a different level of challenge. But, at last, the M3 was feeling like an M3 should.

The wheel-by-wheel regeneration was much more subtle. The i3 already blends electrical and friction braking seamlessly, and the M3 is on a different level, able to use regen to the point of ABS intervention. The left pedal was firm and proportionate, and I had no sense of when one side was handing over to the other. But even under track loadings, most slowing was being done electrically. At the end of my first stint, Wolf, smiling, handed me an infrared temperature reader and invited me to measure the brake temperatures. At the front, the carbon disc was at just 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit), way less than I would expect after 10 minutes of track driving in an 800-hp car that weighs around 5000 pounds. The other advantage of the ability to harvest so much energy is a significant improvement to track range; Wolf claims that for every three laps the car was recuperating enough for another lap at the same pace.

In a recent development, what about the virtual gears? Sorry, the “stages.” These were less convincing. The sounds being piped over the M3’s speakers are loud and engine-like, especially at lower simulated revs, but they grow more otherworldly and sci-fi as the shift lights start to illuminate: I was detecting distinct notes of TIE fighter. M has deliberately taken a different direction from AMG, which has the GT 4-dr doing a full-fledged V-8 impression. BMW’s approach is arguably the more honest one; the M3 isn’t pretending to be something it isn’t.

It has been revealed that but I noticed that the stages also had much less torque modeling than rivals such as Porsche’s E-Shift system in the Taycan, or the pioneering e-Shift in the Hyundai Ioniq 5N, which started this whole game. Beyond the possibility of hitting the M3’s artificial limiter, being in the wrong gear didn’t bring much obvious penalty on track. After a couple of laps of changing with the paddles, I actually went back to Automatic mode, where the virtual gears shift themselves. Which proved that the rising and falling soundtrack does help orientate corner entry speeds. Driving the slow-down lap with both the stepped gears and the speed sound turned off made the M3 prototype suddenly feel like a sensory deprivation chamber.

What was a very limited first drive was clearly aimed at raising anticipation for the finished car more than answering every dynamic question. It was enough to prove that this M3 is a radical shift from its predecessors. But also to validate BMW’s claim that it is set to be the fastest and most powerful M car yet. The prototype also felt at home on a racetrack in a way that EVs very rarely do, and it has clearly been designed with circuit work in mind. This is a very, very different M3—and I’m glad there will still be a more traditional one. But the electric version still feels worthy of its famous badge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda has been getting increasingly serious about electric motorcycles, but if you want to see just how weird the firm thinks the future could get, take a look at the Honda EV Outlier Concept.

I got a chance to see the wild-looking machine in person at EICMA in Milan, where it looked like almost nothing else on the show floor. And that’s exactly the point.

The EV Outlier Concept originally debuted at last year’s Japan Mobility Show as Honda’s attempt to imagine an electric motorcycle that isn’t simply a conventional motorcycle with the engine swapped for a battery and motor. In fact, Honda describes the concept as looking toward the future of electric motorcycles beyond 2030.

The result is certainly unconventional.

This ain’t your grandpa’s SuperCub.

Instead of a centrally mounted motor driving the rear wheel, the EV Outlier uses motors inside both wheels, giving it all-wheel drive and allowing Honda’s designers to completely rethink the rest of the motorcycle’s layout. The battery is housed in that large central black body, while the rider sits extremely low and behind it.

Honda describes the design philosophy with three words: “Gliding, Ecstasy, and Low.” The first refers to the smooth, nearly silent feeling of electric propulsion, while the second describes the instant acceleration and massive torque available from independently controlled front and rear motors. “Low” is more literal: Honda deliberately dropped the rider’s seating and eye position to create an entirely different sensation from a conventional motorcycle.

There’s even a bucket-style backrest designed to support the rider under hard acceleration and let the rider pivot through corners around their hips.

Cool and fun for Honda engineers to play with, but it seems a major no for reality, or at least a different road reality then mine.

Sources indicate that emergency tight swerves for accident avoidance? Nope, gone. Seeing even less of the road, even without a car in front of you, due to being so low? Not good for me nor the deer I don't avoid due to seeing it too late.

Unsprung mass due to hub motors - lots of literature on that topic, so I'll leave that alone.

Up front, traditional mirrors are replaced by cameras, while a wide digital cockpit can display things like lean angle, riding modes, front motor torque adjustment, and what the two wheels are doing in real time.

Will Honda actually build this thing? Almost certainly not exactly as you see it here. That’s what concepts are for.

But the EV Outlier is still interesting as a statement of intent. Honda is obviously still playing around with the freedom that electric drivetrains offer, and the company is asking what motorcycles could become once designers no longer have to work around engines, fuel tanks, transmissions, and traditional drivetrains.

And judging by what I saw at EICMA, Honda’s answer could get pretty wild.

Body hair is completely normal and natural. But if you’re like me and prefer a hair-free look, then take a page from my beauty editor routine and try at-home waxing kits for dolphin-like skin. Dermatologists told me that at-home waxing kits are a worthwhile hair removal method. Unlike shaving, waxing removes hair at the root, whereas a woman's razor blade simply cuts the hair down, says dermatologist Reshmi Kapoor, MD. It’s a bit painful, but the tenderness promptly disappears and the results are so worth the temporary discomfort. Waxing may lead to finer, sparser regrowth over time, so the skin stays hair-free longer than with shaving, says Dr. Kapoor. My underarms are dramatically smoother, lighter, and have fewer ingrown hairs to boot.

At-home waxing kits prevent unsightly razor bumps and are more cost-effective than replacing dull razors and restocking shaving creams. They're also cheaper than professional waxing sessions and save you time from commuting to the waxing studio.

And sure, applying a glob of wax to your body sounds intimidating, but it's surprisingly easy and not as painful as you'd imagine. In our guide to pain-free waxing, experts revealed some helpful advice, like staying hydrated with water and avoiding alcohol before waxing. Another pro tip: skip waxing a few days before your period because you’re dealing with increased sensitivity. Plus, some at-home waxing kits even contain soothing ingredients like aloe vera that are safe for sensitive skin.

Recent findings suggest that with a low-upkeep routine of every four to six weeks, using at-home waxing kits is a no-brainer beauty move. Ahead, Dr. Kapoor and her fellow dermatologists get real about shopping for at-home waxing kits and share their must-have picks. After ordering our editor-tested, dermatologist-approved recommendations, keep reading for more expert tips on post-waxing care.

Industry observers note that out of all the different at-home waxing kits we tried, these wax strips were the easiest to use and the most effective at picking up every single little hair. Flamingo's wax strips won our top spot because they were super simple to apply with very little prep work besides getting the area clean and dry. The soft wax strips are infused with soothing ingredients, like castor seed oil and beeswax, making them ideal for removing fine hair on larger areas, like your arms. Best of all, they’re ready to go whenever you are—no microwave is required. To use them, simply peel apart the strip and apply it, rubbing firmly against your skin to make sure it coats every hair.

We did find the strips a little too major for areas like the face, but you can always cut them down to the correct size with a pair of scissors. Pulling up the wax strip stung quite a bit for Montemayor, but it was over within seconds and the wax effortlessly removed most of her hair on the first go. The strips are very sticky, so she reapplied it to the same area to ensure every last hair was yanked. She especially likes that the post-wax cloth feels very soothing on the skin, and that it helps remove any excess product and stickiness. Montemayor says her redness went away after about an hour, and she was hair-free for a good two weeks after that.

Hard wax kits tend to be messy when they’re applied or removed incorrectly. Remember to always apply a thin, even layer and pull the wax in the opposite direction of hair growth for a seamless waxing experience. However, the results are similar to those you would get at a waxing salon. This Sliick kit comes with a silicone cup and spatula, which makes the heating and application process a breeze. It takes a few rounds of heating and stirring the hard wax to get the right consistency. Once it starts looking like caramel, you’re ready to wax—and the waiting window is totally worth it because the hard wax is easy to maneuver and contains antioxidant-rich acai berry.

The wax itself was easy to spread, but we found that it works best when laid in a thick layer, as thick as a banana peel. Montemayor likes that letting the wax cool completely before pulling the strip gives her a better result. The wax strip came up in one piece, lifting and removing all the hairs in its path. Unlike some of the hard wax kits we tried, this one didn’t leave any wax crumbs behind. Once you’re done waxing, all you have to do is let the wax in the cup and on the applicator dry, and it easily peels off. Montemayor found that after waxing her legs with this kit, it took about 10 days before she noticed the hair growing back.

Pro tip: Remember to dip a fresh stick into the wax pot to avoid introducing bacteria that can cause infections, indicates Strong.

Sources indicate that waxing tends to irritate the skin, but these strips from Billie were the most gentle of all the wax strips we tried. The sticky formula contains added castor oil, avocado oil, and aloe vera to soothe the skin, while the no-rub soft-gel wax attaches to every hair, whether it’s very fine or extra coarse.I used the Billie strips on my legs and underarms, and it was the least painful at-home waxing kit I tried. It’s a little tricky getting all of the hairs of my underarms, but the strips are very sticky, so I can go over the area two or three times and I’m left with smooth, hair-free pits. These strips didn’t leave behind wax on my skin, so cleanup is easy. I’ll just follow up with the included post-wax serum and my redness and minimal irritation are gone.The medium-sized wax strips are great for larger areas like the underarms and legs, but the small strips are too major to use on the upper lip or around the eyebrows. An easy hack is to trim them to fit your face—and with 32 wax strips in total, the $9 kit remains a great value.

Sources indicate that sometimes you just want a product that works for thousands of people. This all-inclusive kit earned a 4.4-star average from more than 38,350 Amazon reviews. More than 26,460 of them were perfect 5-star ratings. Casual.

According to recent reports, so what makes it so impressive among Amazon shoppers? This kit includes quite literally everything you could need for a seamless at-home waxing experience. Waxing beads, an adjustable heat warmer, and 20 sticks for sanitary application? Of course. Skin prep spray and a soothing aftercare spray? Definitely. An instructional booklet with access to advice from a waxing expert via a smartphone app? Yup. It’s like the salon is truly in your bathroom.

Honestly, the biggest con about this device is that it requires some work. But TBH, based on the glowing Amazon reviews it’s a relatively small tradeoff worth the upkeep.

It has been revealed that women with sensitive skin or a low pain tolerance will love this sugaring wax because it’s gentle on the skin without compromising on hair removal. Its screw-on, roll-on applicator makes applying this wax a cinch, allowing you to reach tricky spots, like your chin or underarm, more precisely. Considering the above, it's no surprise that WH contributors love this buy, too. Its compact size is excellent for touch-ups on the go. And it’s a fantastic mess-free alternative that’s easy to apply and smells delicious, claims Jackson. Plus, the wax works on shorter hairs as small as two millimeters, so it removes prickly stubble. While she fully recommends this at-home waxing kit, it’s worth noting that it’s not a hard wax, and it comes with cloth strips that may not cling to thicker hair types.

Sources indicate that these Sally Hansen wax strips are infused with vitamin E and avocado oil for a more nourishing and less irritating waxing experience. The full-size strips are still large enough to cover a good amount of ground—like armpits and legs—and can leave you hair-free for up to eight weeks. You can also snip these strips to fit different areas of your face and body, including your underarms and bikini line.

According to recent reports, before Jackson switched over to laser hair removal, she always kept these strips on hand all the time. She used them for years and suggests putting a dish towel in the microwave for 20 seconds and placing the strip in the towel to warm it up before using it for better results. You can also follow up with a separate oil or serum, since it occasionally leaves a sticky residue on the skin that can be uncomfortable.

These waxing sticks are different from anything else we tried. Despite looking like something you would find in a kid's craft box, these don't play around when it comes to their ability to remove facial hair. The kit comes with two crayon-looking wax sticks, one small and one large. The small one is great for getting the errant hairs around your brows, while the larger stick is the perfect size for removing upper lip hair and peach fuzz on the rest of the face. Montemayor found that the stick made her feel like she had more control over where the wax went, which is especially crucial in sensitive areas like the face.To heat up the wax, all you need is a hair dryer. We recommend using the wax sticks in a bathroom because you’ll need to reheat the sticks often. The sticks are a little stringy, and the application can get messy because you’re trying to catch the wax and apply it before it continues dripping down the stick.

Industry observers note that the hard wax has a pliable texture that snugly fits the curves of your face and can be applied in a nice, thick layer, which makes it easier to remove. We could do two to three swipes with the stick before we needed to blast it with the hair dryer again. The wax formula itself was very gentle and didn’t leave any sticky residue behind or tug at the top layer of skin. Overall, it was mostly painless because you’re working in such small sections. Once the stick dries, you can tuck it away for safekeeping and reuse it again the next time you need to remove your facial hair. We particularly like these sticks because they're travel-friendly, too. You can definitely throw them in a toiletry bag on your next weekend getaway.

With only three key factors to keep in mind, shopping for at-home waxing kits is refreshingly simple.

Before waxing, you should know there are two types of waxes: hard and soft.

If you want to use something stripless, go for hard wax. It adheres to the hair follicle (versus the skin), hardens, and can be removed on its own, eliminating the need for paper strips. For some, it may even feel less painful than soft wax, so it's great for sensitive skin, claims dermatologist Nazanin Saedi, MD. The only caveat is that you may have to apply it several times in the same area to make sure all the hairs you target are removed.

Soft wax, on the other hand, is soft and applied in a thin layer. A paper strip is then used to adhere and remove the wax. Often, the top layer of skin is also removed, so it can be irritating for people with sensitive skin.

According to recent reports, ideally, beginners should look for kits that contain everything they need to get the job done—wax, strips, and finishing oil, at minimum. Novices may also appreciate waxing kits that come with pre-loaded strips, since they're less messy and require less precision. The tradeoff? You're limited to the size of the included strips, so look for kits with multiple sizes if you're targeting different areas of the body. Larger strips are fantastic for your legs, while small strips are practical for your face.

It's important to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin. If you have sensitive skin, look for waxing kits that include skin-soothing ingredients, like castor and almond oils or aloe. And whatever you use, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. This will allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

Industry observers note that for the past year, Women’s Health contributors and I, including Sabrina Talbert, Jasmine Gomez, Danielle Jackson, and Cristina Montemayor, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated at-home waxing kits. Our team consulted dermatologists Blair Murphy-Rose, MD, Nazanin Saedi, MD, and Uchenna Okereke, MD, for pre-waxing advice and aftercare instructions to prevent irritation and promote healthy skin. Then, we got our hands on the kits and tested them in the comfort of our own homes, evaluating attributes like ease of use, comfort, results, and overall value. Of the 25 at-home waxing kits tested, the seven on this list delivered the best results in our in-depth evaluations.

Industry observers note that at-home waxing removes body hair conveniently and cost-effectively, and the best kits do it quickly while minimizing pain and irritation. So, if you’re ready to ditch the razors, check out this list of the best waxing kits, tested by dermatologists and WH editors.

It has been revealed that after waxing, you can prevent ingrown hairs from forming and minimize irritation immediately afterward by applying cool aloe to soothe skin, and sticking to loose clothes that won't create friction. "Aloe vera has anti-inflammatory properties that help soothe sunburned skin, while glycerin specifically can help to boost hydration levels to restore the skin's moisture barrier," dermatologist Divya Shokeen, MD, previously told WH in our guide to the best aloe vera gel. Some kits also come with nourishing oils and wipes to help minimize any post-wax irritation.

Before you head off to wax unwanted hair, these are a few other tips you should keep in mind.

Industry observers note that waxing removes hair by lifting it out at the root. With traditional waxing, hot wax is applied to skin and the hair is pulled off in the opposite direction of the way it's growing. The key word here and what can make at-home waxing dangerous is that it's hot.

“Hot wax can burn the skin—and it is a particularly dangerous type of burn because the hot product adheres to the skin,” says Dr. Murphy-Rose. Always make sure you're following the heating directions closely and that you hold your hand over the wax after it's been heated to gauge the temperature before applying it to your skin.

Sources indicate that then, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. "That way you can check the temperature, but also see how your skin reacts," says Dr. Saedi. Testing a product will also allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. “It's notable to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin," says Dr. Murphy-Rose. You should also avoid any ingredients you have a known allergy or sensitivity to. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

In a recent development, "Hot wax tends to adhere the strongest, so while it may remove hairs more efficiently, it can also stick to skin more and pull off those top layers of the skin as it's also pulling out your hair,” claims Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Waxing exfoliates the top layer of skin and is more likely to cause hyperpigmentation a.k.a. dark spots, says Dr. Okereke. She says to think of the skin after waxing like a fresh, pink wound. "Ultraviolet rays are attracted to wounds, making the freshly waxed skin more susceptible to darkening as melanin (the dark pigment in skin) floods the area to try and protect it." Luckily, there is a simple fix: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen! Better yet, keep that fresh skin out of the sun completely for at least a few days.

It has been revealed that you'll also want to avoid any extra exfoliation, like retinol, chemical peels, and microdermabrasion, a few days prior and a few days following your at-home wax. A few other good things to know before getting started: Always wax on clean skin to avoid bacterial contamination in pores and make sure your hairs are long enough (at least 1/4 of an inch) to be grabbed by the wax.

In a recent development, the key to preventing ingrown hairs (an all too common downside of waxing for many) is to get the full hair follicle. The best way to do this is by keeping your skin taut and pulling the wax strip in the opposite direction of the way that your hair grows.

Recent findings suggest that sugaring, aka sugared wax or sugar gel, is generally safer because it’s applied to skin at room temperature (read: no risk of burning skin) and warms up with body heat. “Sugared ‘wax’ is not truly wax,” Dr. Murphy-Rose states. Rather, it’s a combination of sugar, lemon juice, and water. Some brands will infuse glycerin, fragrance, honey, or essential oils. Regardless of which brand you opt for, sugaring is water-soluble and easily rinses off the skin compared to hot wax, she says.

According to recent reports, sugaring and threading remove the hair follicle from the root but with less exfoliating, offering a gentler process, Dr. Okereke claims. Though she warns that she's also had patients with coily-textured hair that still develop ingrown hairs and scarring from sugaring as well. The bottom line: "If you know you're prone to hyperpigmentation, ingrown hairs, or scarring, see a dermatologist to discuss the best hair removal practices for you," says Dr. Okereke.

Bitcoin Breaks Below $60K as Crypto Fear Index Hits Worst Level Since February

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin broke below $60,000 on Friday, plunging through a major psychological price level as the selloff gathered pace after Anthropic’s stock market debut.
  • The daily chart demonstrates BTC at $59,703.72 , down 3.55% for the session after touching a low of $59,300.
  • According to recent reports, the Fear and Greed Index chart dipped to 9, a reading classified as “extreme fear” and its lowest since February.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin broke below $60,000 on Friday, plunging through a major psychological price level as the selloff gathered pace after Anthropic’s stock market debut.

The daily chart demonstrates BTC at $59,703.72 , down 3.55% for the session after touching a low of $59,300.

According to recent reports, the Fear and Greed Index chart dipped to 9, a reading classified as “extreme fear” and its lowest since February. For reference, the index was at 18 a week ago and a neutral 51 a month earlier.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

According to recent reports, the indicator tracks crypto market sentiment on a scale from zero, or maximum fear, to 100, or extreme greed, using market data rather than individual investor surveys. Its 2026 low was 5 on February 5, compared with a yearly high of 82 on August 26.

The selling went well beyond Bitcoin. Ethereum fell 4.24%, Solana lost 6.36%, BNB slid 4.38% and XRP declined 5.53% over the same period.

Industry observers note that forced selling added to the pressure. As Decrypt reported earlier Friday, roughly $727 million in leveraged crypto positions had been liquidated over 24 hours, about 86% of them bullish bets, while U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $582.2 million on Thursday.

Spot fund withdrawals did not begin with Anthropic’s IPO. By Thursday, roughly $2.9 billion in U.S. Bitcoin ETF outflows for November, alongside higher Treasury yields and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut Thursday at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 IPO price, before closing at $97.17. Friday brought another decline for the Claude developer, with the stock almost losing all the prime it gained after its IPO.

The listing raised $81.34 billion through the public offering, but enthusiasm for Anthropic shares did not carry over to the companies building the AI boom.

Industry observers note that friday’s market heatmap demonstrates tech stock suffering in the middle of mostly green pastures. Nvidia down 3.78%, Broadcom is down 5.65%, AMD declining 5.06% and memory-chip maker Micron dropping 6.51%. Meta fell 2.21%, adding to pressure on companies spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

Other major stocks were doing better. Alphabet rose 2.81%, Microsoft gained 0.50% and Apple edged up 0.25%, while healthcare stocks Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson rose 1.21% and 1.78%, respectively. Walmart added 2.91% and Visa climbed 1.34%.

But it was not a uniform crash across the S&P 500. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was falling more sharply than the broader index, while pockets of healthcare, consumer, and financial shares remained green.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s daily chart turned more decisively bearish after the break below $60,000. Its 50-day exponential moving average, or EMA, was below the 200-day EMA, a death-cross configuration, and spot prices were trading beneath both lines. That confirms sustained downside momentum rather than a brief intraday dip.

According to recent reports, the relative strength index, or RSI, had fallen into the teens, far below the 30 threshold usually associated with oversold conditions. The average directional index, or ADX, climbed to 43.7, signaling a strong trend, with the chart’s directional readings favoring sellers. Oversold does not mean a bounce is guaranteed.

The longer-range chart puts the $60,000 breakdown in context. Bitcoin traded around this area several times in 2024 and returned to it during the mid-2026 retreat, making it a visible historical price zone as well as a round-number threshold.

With $60,000 giving way, the roughly $58,000–$59,000 support area near the mid-2026 lows comes into focus. If that zone fails, the next notable historical demand area is around $55,000–$56,000, followed by the $50,000 region marked by the deeper 2024 selloff.

For bulls, $60,000 is now the first level to hold. The next hurdle is $62,000–$62,500, followed by $65,000 and heavier resistance near $68,000–$70,000. A brief bounce back above $60,000 would not, by itself, reverse the bearish trend.

According to recent reports, as of right now, Bitcoin had touched $59,300.13, confirming that sellers had pushed below the $60,000 support zone. The next test is whether that level becomes resistance on a rebound.

Elvis Presley at Home: Tour the King’s Private Life in 14 Photos, From the Heartland to Hawaii

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elvis Presley is one of those icons so permanently etched into the fabric of American popular culture that it seems, nearly half a century after his death, as if he will live forever.
  • Today, the museum, which encompasses Presley’s gravesite, former home, and a collection of mementos of Presley’s rock-and-roll career, stands as a stirring reminder of one man’s life, as he grew from a beloved child to poverty-stricken parents to, arguably, the most famous man in the world.
  • Recent findings suggest that presley and his parents pose for a photo at home in Tupelo, Mississippi, circa 1945—the year before he received his first guitar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elvis Presley is one of those icons so permanently etched into the fabric of American popular culture that it seems, nearly half a century after his death, as if he will live forever. While Presley also had homes in California, and famously lived in Germany during his stint in the US Army, it is Graceland that is most strongly associated with the late musician. The rock and roller’s Memphis residence where he lived for 20 years and where he died at the age of 42, Graceland is America’s second-most-visited residence, behind the White House. Every year, an average of 600,000 people flock to the residence turned museum, which opened to the public in 1982.

Today, the museum, which encompasses Presley’s gravesite, former home, and a collection of mementos of Presley’s rock-and-roll career, stands as a stirring reminder of one man’s life, as he grew from a beloved child to poverty-stricken parents to, arguably, the most famous man in the world. Below, we’re rounding up photos of the legendary musician at his (almost) equally famous home, and other places he rested his pompadoured head.

The Presleys at home in Tupelo, around 1945.

Recent findings suggest that presley and his parents pose for a photo at home in Tupelo, Mississippi, circa 1945—the year before he received his first guitar. The future king of rock and roll was born nearby, in a two-room house built by his father, grandfather, and uncle on January 8, 1935. That house, now a museum, was repossessed three years later, and the family bounced around other homes in the area before moving to Memphis when Presley was 13 years old. There, the family lived in Lauderdale Courts, a public housing project.

Presley relaxing at 1034 Audubon Drive.

In March 1956, riding high on the success of Presley’s first RCA single, “Heartbreak Hotel,” the family became homeowners for the very first time. A house of her own had always been Gladys’s dream, and her 21-year-old son made it a reality when he paid $29,250 for 1034 Audubon Drive, a low-rise, seven-room ranch house with four bedrooms. Gladys likened it to living in a palace. They also added a backyard pool–at the time, it was the only one on the street. While most wealthy men of his tender age might have set their parents up with a house before shimmying off to live the bachelor’s life elsewhere, this wasn’t Elvis’s style; living together as a close-knit trio was always part of his master plan.

Elvis Presley and a friend chat in the back yard of his house at 1034 Audubon Drive in 1956.

On their quiet, leafy street in the rapidly growing East Memphis, the Presleys were soon living the suburban dream. Things might well have stayed that way too, had Elvis’s star not reached stratospheric heights over the following months. By the summer of 1956, Elvis had recorded smash hits “Hound Dog” and “Don’t Be Cruel.” His first feature film, Love Me Tender, premiered later that year, making him a bona fide movie star.

Swarms of fans soon crowded the sidewalk outside the family home day and night. Elvis had initially slept in the front bedroom, which was decorated with pink floral wallpaper, but eventually moved into the master bedroom at the back of the house after fans began peering through his window for a glimpse of their idol. To restore some shred of privacy, the Presleys had a brick and metal fence installed around the property. Elvis is pictured above leaning against the railings, chatting to a friend in his backyard.

Elvis and his parents relax on the patio.

According to recent reports, elvis kicks his feet up alongside his parents on the Audubon Drive home’s patio in this July 1956 photo. The Presleys had moved to this upper-middle-class neighborhood just four months prior. During their residency, the family tried to fit in with their neighbors in the affluent community to the best of their ability; Gladys let local kids cool off in their newly installed pool and made them peanut butter sandwiches, while Elvis would take them for a spin on the back of his gleaming motorcycle. But it soon became clear that Elvis’s fame would put a strain on life in the area. Perhaps it was when Hollywood star Natalie Wood came to stay at the house on Audubon—which turned the street into a circus as fans gathered to watch her pose outside on Elvis’s motorcycle—or the hot dog stand that set up outside that magically appeared to feed the constant stream of fans. The final straw may have been when a helicopter landed on the vacant lot beside the house to collect Elvis, leaving the neighbors well and truly shaken up.

By March 1957 the Presleys had packed their bags and moved on from the house on Audubon, restoring a relative sense of peace to the quaint suburban neighborhood. The family may have spent just a year at their Audubon Drive home, but it was a pivotal chapter in Elvis’s life story, marking a transition between the transient lifestyle of his impoverished childhood and the security and permanence he would find in his next home: Graceland.

The fresh homeowner with his hand on one of Graceland’s now iconic columns.

Presley skyrocketed to stardom in the mid ’50s, garnering a recording contract with RCA Records. This newfound wealth meant the boy whose home was repossessed, and who lived in public housing, could now buy the lavish house of his dreams for himself and his parents. In March 1957, the 22-year-old “Hound Dog” singer paid $102,500 for Graceland, which would remain his primary residence for the rest of his life. The home had been built in 1939 on a plot of land the original owner named after his daughter, Grace; the name stuck. Here, Presley leans on one of the home’s pillars shortly after the purchase.

Elvis in wrought iron, and in the flesh, at the gates to Graceland.

The musician poses in front of Graceland’s famous wrought iron music note gate in April 1957, around the time he had it installed. Abe Saucer designed the gates—which feature life-size images of Elvis playing guitar amid musical notes—and had them custom-built by John Dillars Jr. At the time, the property spanned 13.8 acres, with the mansion clocking in at over 10,200 square feet—later, Elvis would expand it to 17,500 square feet and 23 rooms, with additions including the famous Jungle Room.

A palace fit for the king of rock and roll.

Recent findings suggest that the “Burning Love” singer walks in front of Graceland, circa 1957. Early design details that Presley added to the Colonial Revival estate included a custom 15-foot-long blue metallic sofa (later reupholstered in white), a pink flagstone wall around the property, a kidney-shaped swimming pool, and a full-size soda fountain. In his initial renovations, Presley spent $500,000 (over $5 million in today’s dollars).

It has been revealed that in March 1958, Presley was drafted into the US Army. He is pictured in his off-post home in Bad Nauheim, Germany, in January 1960, shortly after being promoted to sergeant. It was here that the 24-year-old singer met a 14-year-old Priscilla Beaulieu, when a friend of his who had spotted Priscilla at a restaurant brought her to a party at Presley’s place to introduce them. To this day, the home at 14 Goethestrasse is still a landmark for fans.

Elvis and his father mourning after the death of Gladys.

In a recent development, elvis and his father Vernon on the steps of Graceland in August 1958, shortly after the deathof his beloved mother, Gladys. The two had been exceptionally close, and her loss was toprove a devastating turning point. Elvis had always believed that the purpose of his extraordinary success was to provide his parents with the security and comfort they had been denied during his childhood. Buying them a home, and ultimately one as grand as Graceland, had been central to that vision. But now, just as he had achieved everything he had worked for, his mother was gone. With the loss of her unwavering love and support, it was as though a curtain had fallen on Elvis’s life. The young man who had once seemed so certain of his place in the world would never quite be the same again.

In March, 1960, Presley was discharged from the Army and returned home to Graceland, but it was a sadder and lonelier place, since Gladys died while he was in basic training. Here, he stands with his Rolls-Royce in front of Graceland, circa 1960. The Jailhouse Rock star had an affinity for slick cars, but it wasn’t the only mode of transportation he enjoyed at the estate. Priscilla Beaulieu, who came to visit him at Graceland in 1962 and moved in the following year, wrote in her 1985 memoir Elvis and Me that he “turned Graceland into a private playground for us all. He’d have gun-shooting contests and also ‘screaming thrill rides’ when he’d pack several people into his custom-built golf cart and race around the grounds at top speed.”.

Elvis and Priscilla were married in Las Vegas on May 1, 1967. He was 32; she was 21. Exactly nine months later, on February 1, 1968, their first and only child, Lisa Marie Presley, was born.

Priscilla and Elvis brought a tropical design aesthetic home from their vacations in Hawaii.

Hawaii became a bit of a home away from home for Presley following his 1961 film, Blue Hawaii. He returned often to vacation there, including in 1968, when this snapshot was taken. The “Don’t Be Cruel” singer was so inspired by the tropical locale that he added a tiki-inspired space to Graceland. Now known as the Jungle Room, the kitschy den features wood-paneled walls, green shag carpeting on the floor and ceiling, carved wooden furniture with faux fur upholstery, and a built-in rock waterfall feature.

Priscilla, Elvis, and baby Lisa Marie relax at home.

According to recent reports, the Presleys relax in Graceland’s pool area, circa 1970. He had added the kidney-shaped pool and flagstone patio to the property in 1957. This snapshot shares a relaxed, happy moment, but life with Elvis wasn’t all pool parties for Priscilla. In Elvis and Me, Priscilla wrote frankly about their controversial relationship: “When we met, I had just turned 14. The first six months I spent with him were filled with tenderness and affection. Blinded by love, I saw none of his faults or weaknesses. He was to become the passion of my life. He taught me everything: how to dress, how to walk, how to apply makeup and wear my hair, how to behave, how to return love—his way. Over the years he became my father, husband, and very nearly God.”.

Lisa Marie and her father at Graceland.

In a recent development, elvis and Lisa Marie are shown here on the porch of Graceland in the early 1970s. Lisa Marie later recalled the curious rhythms of life at the mansion. Her father was nocturnal, she explained, and the household rarely got going before about two in the afternoon. Lisa Marie remembered fondly hearing the rotary phone ring and being summoned upstairs to spend quality time with her dad in his bedroom. “I would just sit up there, and he’d talk to me and ask what I was doing while he watched one of his 17 televisions or listened to records,” she stated in her memoir, From Here to the Great Unknown, co-written with her daughter Riley Keough. On occasion, Elvis would come downstairs and take the family and their friends out for an impromptu evening at the movie theater, shutting it down so they could watch a James Bond film or The Pink Panther.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

In a recent development, one of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the latest R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

Sources indicate that though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the tech giant’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the massive machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

It has been revealed that in addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT states the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

We’ll post an patch once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this major burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

A Better Airport Outfit Starts With the Basics

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • Recent findings suggest that airports can be a bit intimidating.
  • And while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that airports can be a bit intimidating. You’ve got the TSA line to worry about, but more importantly, you have your outfit to figure out. Unfortunately, some people judge what you’re wearing while traveling (it’s me, I’m people). But I also don’t think looking presentable has to be that hard. Some guys show up in full sweats, looking like they're about to spend the next six hours in bed. Others dress like they're heading straight from baggage claim to a dinner reservation. Personally, I think there's a happy medium somewhere in there. You should be comfortable enough to sleep through your flight, but you also shouldn't have to change your entire outfit the second you land. From comfortable pants and breathable T-shirts to stylish sneakers, these are the essentials worth packing for your next flight.

And while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport. We’ve got stretchy trousers that look pretty darn good, a solid pair of sneakers, and layers that work alone or together. It's about finding clothes that do a little bit of everything, especially if you like to travel light.

If you’re looking to spruce up your fit for your next flight (and to become someone’s airport crush), here’s what to know.

I'm not saying you can't wear jeans on a plane, but why would you when you have so many more comfortable alternatives? You'll be sitting for hours, probably in a seat that doesn't give you much room to move, so the last thing you want is a waistband digging into your stomach. Look for pants with a little stretch, breathable fabrics, and a relaxed fit that won't feel restrictive when you're sitting down. Brands like Vuori and DUER have gotten particularly good at making pants that feel like loungewear without necessarily looking like it. And if you're committed to sweatpants, that's perfectly fine, too. Just go for a pair with a cleaner, more structured fit.

Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Relaxed Sweatpant.

Nike Club Open Hem Brushed Fleece Pants.

You really don't need to overthink your airport T-shirt. A good cotton tee will do just fine, especially if it's something you already wear regularly. Personally, I'd avoid anything too tight or made from a heavy fabric, since airports and airplanes can get surprisingly stuffy. A slightly relaxed fit gives you more room to move and makes layering easier, too. I tend to gravitate toward simple, solid-colored tees because they go with practically anything. Uniqlo's AIRism Cotton Oversized T-Shirt is a good example of something that's affordable, comfortable, and easy to dress up or down depending on what else you're wearing.

Mack Weldon Pima Long Sleeve T-Shirt.

Everlane The Essential Organic Crew.

I don't care if you're flying to Miami in the middle of July; bring a sweatshirt. Airplane cabins have a habit of feeling like refrigerators, and I'd much rather have an extra layer than spend an entire flight shivering. A good crewneck or hoodie is probably all you need, preferably something soft that isn't too bulky to stuff into your bag when you're not wearing it. I'm partial to oversized sweatshirts for traveling, though you don't need to go so big that you're drowning in fabric. Something like Alo's Accolade Crewneck works well because you can wear it with sweatpants or a nicer pair of trousers. And honestly, if you're desperate, a sweatshirt can always double as a makeshift pillow.

Abercrombie SwEssential Popover 2.0 Hoodie.

Todd Snyder Champion Relaxed French Terry Crewneck.

Eddie Bauer Micro Polar Fleece Lined Pullover Hoodie.

Depending on where you're headed, a lightweight jacket might be one of the more useful things you bring. I'm not talking about a huge puffer or anything that'll take up half your carry-on. Think windbreakers, chore jackets, and lightweight layers that you can easily throw over a T-shirt or sweatshirt. If you're traveling somewhere with unpredictable weather, a technical jacket from Patagonia or Arc'teryx makes sense. Otherwise, a simple chore jacket from somewhere like Quince or Gap can make an otherwise basic airport outfit look a little more put-together. Plus, you'll probably wear it during the trip anyway, so it's one less thing to pack.

Quince 100% Organic Herringbone Twill Shirt Jacket.

Arc’teryx Atom Insulated Jacket.

Recent findings suggest that between getting to the airport, navigating security, and walking what feels like three miles to your gate, you'll probably spend more time on your feet than you realize. That's why I'd prioritize comfortable sneakers over anything else when putting together an airport outfit. You want a pair with good cushioning, enough support, and ideally something easy to slip on and off. Latest Balance, Hoka, and On all make sneakers that fit the bill, though I'd stick with a pair you've already broken in rather than trying something new on travel day. And since you're probably only bringing one or two pairs of shoes on your trip, bonus points if they match the rest of your wardrobe.

On The Roger Centre Tennis Court Shoe.

You really don't need much here. In fact, I'd argue the best airport outfits are pretty simple. But a few accessories can make even a basic T-shirt-and-sweatpants combination feel more intentional. A classic Yankees cap from '47 is great for early flights when you don't feel like doing your hair, and a good pair of sunglasses is always useful when you're heading somewhere sunny. I also like wearing a watch when I travel, mostly because I don't want to keep pulling out my phone to check the time. None of these things are essential, obviously, but they're easy ways to make the outfit feel a little more like your own.

Tifosi Veloce Sports Sunglasses.

Seiko Analog Green Dial Automatic Silver Stainless Steel Watch.

Breaking: Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.
  • The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.
  • We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

It has been revealed that for context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar indicates the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

It has been revealed that up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker states this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only highlights itself when the car is driving autonomously.

Industry observers note that the rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”.

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”.

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

In a recent development, the interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

It has been revealed that but the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar states it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the manufacturer’s head of interior design, put it plainly:.

Sources indicate that “As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”.

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

It has been revealed that the cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

Recent findings suggest that the four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

Sources indicate that the cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

In a recent development, now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four upcoming models Polestar looks to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

It has been revealed that europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this upcoming head of design.

In a recent development, the proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, massive haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

It has been revealed that I have loved Polestar from the day they debuted. Every car they design is a work of art and I love their commitment to transparency and sustainablitity. The 2023 Polestar 2 is still one of my favorite cars I've ever owned. I've driven the 3 and the 4 and both were fantastic. The fit and finish, ride and build quality, and NVH were all excellent. The upgraded 3 was probably going to be my next car in 2027 until they were forced to withdraw from the US. I think their future with the upcoming 2 and 7 are bright and I'm still hoping (though I'm not holding my breath) that they will return to the US at some point. If the 5 was available here, I'd buy it today.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Sources indicate that polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

According to recent reports, now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.
